note.title: Verxoslava Vsevolodovna
note.p: The daughter of Vsevolod M′stislavič and great–granddaughter of Monomax, Verxoslava is mentioned by name as having been sent to Poland in 1137. Hypatian Chronicle, s.a. 1137. Though no reason for the trip is mentioned, such trips were almost exclusively for the purpose of marriage. Unfortunately, no source that I have found records the person she married, but Baumgarten lists him as Bolesław IV of Poland, as does Balzer. Baumgarten, "Généalogies," table V; and Balzer, Genealogia Piastów, 158–60. However, Stanisław Smolka, whom Balzer cites in other instances, identifies Bolesław IV’s wife as a daughter of either M′stislav or Jaropolk Volodimerič, and thus a granddaughter of Monomax. Stanisław Smolka, Mieszko Stary i jego wiek (Warsaw: Geberthnera i wolfa, 1881), 213, genealogical table. Smolka’s identification, which he characterizes as tenuous, becomed even more problematic with his identification of her name as Anastazya. It thus seems that Smolka is incorrect, and though we have no primary source evidence to support the identification of Verxoslava’s spouse as Bolesław IV, he seems the most likely match under the circumstances, especially considering the marriages that followed.

The marriage of a M′stislavna and a Piast was an important step in binding the two ruling families closer together, but it was actually much more than that. For years the Piasts had been allies of the Izjaslaviči, but after the destruction of Izjaslavič power, and the death of Sbyslava Svjatopolkovna, in the early twelfth century, it was time for new alliances to be made. The death of Sbyslava is particularly relevant as she was wife to Bolesław III and mother to Władysław II. After her death, Bolesław III remarried and had more children, including Bolesław IV. The stepbrothers (Władysław II on one side v. Bolesław IV, Mieszko and Henryk on the other) would war for control of the Piast territories through the mid-twelfth century. As will be seen below in the marriage of Zvenislava Vsevolodovna, each side of this Piast struggle made Volodimeroviči connections. Bolesław IV married into the M′stislaviči while Władysław II will marry into the Ol′goviči (through his son Bolesław the Tall). The division in Piasts then mirrored the division amongst the Volodimeroviči and the basis for mutual assistance in the coming wars was created. This starts immediately upon the marriage of Zvenislava Vsevolodovna (discussed below) in 1142 when Vsevolod Olgovič sends troops to assist his zjat′ Wladysław II. Hypatian Chronicle, s.a. 1142. While in 1149, Izjaslav M′stislavič was able to call on his brothers-in-law Bolesław IV, Mieszko, and Henryk to aid him in his own internal Rusian struggles. Hypatian Chronicle, s.a. 1149. This is a particularly interesting event in regards to dynastic marriage as Izjaslav called upon Polish, Hungarian, and Bohemian help, all through familial connections, and actually received help from all of them. As the M′stislaviči would win in Rus’, the side of Bolesław IV would win in Poland, though neither were lasting.
